articles.title: ‘12.12: The Day’ Director Kim Sung-soo Says AI ‘Shows What’s in Your Imagination’
articles.summary: Kim Sung-soo, director of Korean box office hit “12.12: The Day,” once saw AI as a destroyer of the film industry. Speaking Sunday at a session hosted by Kling AI at the Busan International Film Festival’s Asian Contents & Film Market, he described how it has instead become part of his craft.
body: Kim was joined by Harry Hyun, director and CEO of AI production company MooAm; Chinese animation director Li Wei, co-director of “Jiang Ziya”; and Lee Sangwook, producer and team manager at MBC C&I’s AI Contents Lab.

Li made a similar case for animation. Presenting a trailer for “Born of the Tide,” a 105-minute AI-animated feature about China’s boat-dwelling Tanka community, he said the technology works best at the trial-and-error stage: concept designs that once took enormous time to draw by hand can now be visualized quickly and shared with the team. “AI can generate many things, but the choice and the details all come down to the director,” he said.

Hyun agreed that filmmaking skill is what makes the difference. “Faces look identical, sets look identical, lighting looks identical,” she said of AI output made without it. That is why MooAm looks for AI artists who have directed at least one live-action short.

articles.title: Keanu Reeves-Voiced Stop-Motion Samurai Film ‘Hidari’ Looks for New Partner After U.S. Talks Stall
articles.summary: Japan’s Dwarf Studios is looking for a new partner for “Hidari,” the stop-motion samurai film voiced by Keanu Reeves, after talks with a U.S. company that offered to fund the entire budget in exchange for all rights stalled, producer Matsumoto Noriko told an audience at the Busan International Film…
body: Questry has set up a special purpose company for “Hidari” so that overseas and local investors can put money into the film side by side. Ibe said the project shows why development money matters. Dwarf made a pilot short in 2023 at its own risk, partly through crowdfunding, and the pilot traveled far enough to bring Reeves aboard. Questry now wants to back pilots and development-stage work, which in Japan studios and creators usually pay for themselves.

In Korea, by contrast, investors, distributors and producers play separate roles, and Ibe said producers often take around 40% of profit after recoupment. “How you raise money decides how you share it,” he said.

Ibe’s presentation described the committee as a well-built system that works very well for titles made in Japan for Japan. It can still serve titles sold worldwide if overseas rights are planned from day one, he said, but the fit gets worse the more global a project is. A co-production with few Japanese windows to sell gives Japanese companies little reason to invest, and only Japanese companies can sit on a committee. Overseas sales made up 56% of anime industry revenue in 2024, up from 20% in 2014, he noted.

articles.title: ‘Between Two Lovers’ Review: Nanako Hirose’s Contentious Family Drama Examines an Ill-Fated Throuple
articles.summary: The sophomore feature from Hirokazu Kore-eda protégé Nanako Hirose, “Between Two Lovers” tackles a variety of potential hot-button issues, from polyamorous relationships to same-sex parenting, in its contemporary Japanese setting.
body: Masami Nagasawa is applaudably unlikable as an adulterous author with a resistance to motherhood, who invites her husband and girlfriend to conceive a child together in a tantalizing proposition that pulls too many of its punches.

Little does he know, Uta has also been involved in a passionate six-year affair with her female editor, Junna (Shizuka Ishibashi), and happily flits back and forth between her two homes, beds, and lovers. Junna is eager to become a mother, although several legal barriers prevent her from accessing sperm donations or fertility treatment. She also wants Uta to accept her sexuality and get a divorce, so that they can live together openly.

body: What's it like to be the main character of an online scandal?
That's one of the questions raised in a new documentary about Lisa Manobal – one quarter of K-pop phenomenon Blackpink and a breakout star of TV show The White Lotus.
The film captures an unfolding controversy, as leaked videos show Blackpink using racial slurs when they were teenage trainees in the K-pop system.
The clips, which emerged last year, showed the band covering US rap songs during rehearsals. Explicit language, including the n-word, was left uncensored.

articles.title: Netflix Has Used AI on About 300 Titles, but “Human Touch Is Critical,” Exec Says in Busan
articles.summary: Netflix’s Asia-Pacific production head Sung Q Lee, ‘The Outlaws’ director Kang Yun-sung and Wētā FX's Kimball Thurston discussed creative possibilities, production savings and the limits of AI at the streamer’s Creative Asia event in Busan.
body: Netflix has already used AI in various capacities on about 300 titles, one of its senior production executives said Saturday during an industry discussion at the Busan International Film Festival.
Sung Q Lee, Netflix’s senior director of production for Asia-Pacific, said the technology was being deployed across the filmmaking process, but stressed the importance of preserving human creativity.

Lee was speaking at Netflix’s annual Creative Asia event, presented in partnership with the Busan International Film Festival. The panel, co-hosted with the Motion Picture Association, also featured Korean filmmaker Kang Yun-sung, the director of The Outlaws and an enthusiastic adopter of AI tools, and Kimball Thurston, chief technology officer at Wētā FX.

articles.title: ‘New Girl’ Stars Reunite — in a Slightly Different Way Than Max Greenfield Claimed
articles.summary: Zooey Deschanel, Max Greenfield, Jake Johnson, Lamorne Morris, Hannah Simone and Damon Wayans Jr. stepped out together as they were honored at the Chrysalis Butterfly Ball on Saturday.
body: The stars came together at the Chrysalis Butterfly Ball in Los Angeles, where together they received the Rising Phoenix Award and Greenfield served as the evening’s host. The event was put on in support of Southern California nonprofit Chrysalis, which helps individuals navigate obstacles on their path to meaningful employment.

Greenfield’s viral moment was a hot topic of conversation at the event, as Deschanel teased while the group accepted their award, “We especially would like to thank Max, who while organizing this announced that an actual New Girl reunion was happening and he made our lives so very annoying.”

“Now is probably not the most appropriate time to apologize for this but yes, that’s something that happened and I am sorry. It did, however, bring a lot of attention to Chrysalis and what we are doing here tonight, accidentally,” Greenfield responded. “When the six of us reunite — six actors, none of whom graduated college except apparently Hannah, which does make a lot of sense; Jake says he did graduate college, which no one believes — but when we come together, remarkably people pay attention and people show up, and we are so grateful that you showed up tonight.”

articles.title: ‘Treasure Island’ Review: David Oyelowo and Hayley Atwell Can Only Breathe So Much Life Into MGM+’s Handsome but Undercooked Pirate Adventure
articles.summary: Jack Huston and Tom Sweet also star in the reimagining of Robert Louis Stevenson's classic novel, about a young man's ocean-traversing quest for buried treasure.
body: You cannot fault Treasure Island, MGM+’s new take on the Robert Louis Stevenson classic, for a lack of effort. Where some adaptations of beloved literary works might be content to recreate the source material beat for beat, creator Robert Murphy reimagines it wholesale.

It takes a while to reveal its shortcomings, however. Initially, there’s plenty to be intrigued by. Our hero to come of age is Jim Hawkins (Tom Sweet), a sweet-natured fellow with the height of a man, the acne-spotted cheeks of a teenager, the wide-eyed innocence of a boy and, most importantly to the plot, the eidetic memory of almost no one of any age. Jim and his widowed mother, Bess ( Hayley Atwell ), are barely scraping by running a bustling tavern, even with the occasional extra coin they pull in by having drunkards bet on Jim’s gift for perfect recall.

articles.title: 6 Crime Shows That Are Better Because You Already Know the Killer
articles.summary: Most crime shows live by the rule of keeping the killer hidden until the very end. This means that the mystery around that big reveal does most of the heavy lifting. However, there is a certain thrill that comes with letting the audience in on the secret.
body: Feel free to connect with him or check out his work. He's everywhere — Upwork, YouTube, Spotify, SoundCloud, Collider, LinkedIn, Instagram.

Instead of chasing the story, the audience gets to sit inside it and watch every character on screen operate with half the information they have. Nothing about the plot has changed, but everything about how it lands has. This is a list of acclaimed crime shows that use this storytelling to make for some of the most rewarding watches in the genre, exactly because they reveal their killer to the viewers.

Columbo built its identity around subverting what viewers expected from murder mysteries back in the day. That’s because most episodes of the show begin by revealing exactly who committed the crime in question, how they executed their plan, and what their alibi is going to be. Then, Lieutenant Columbo ( Peter Falk ) arrives to kick off his investigation and begins noticing details the murderer assumed nobody would care about. This inverted structure was definitely strange in the beginning, but soon enough, the audience realized how fun it really was.
